design_detail: Prospective population birth cohort (Dunedin Multidisciplinary Health and Development Study, New Zealand: 1,037 children born April 1972 to March 1973, 91% of eligible births). Exposure: the number of five past-year assessment windows (ages 18, 21, 26, 32 and 38) at which a person met DSM criteria for cannabis dependence on the Diagnostic Interview Schedule, and in parallel the number at which cannabis was used on 4 or more days a week. Outcome: within-person change in full-scale IQ from childhood (WISC-R, mean of ages 7, 9, 11 and 13, before cannabis use) to age 38 (WAIS-IV), in SD units; tests given only at 38 (WMS-III, Trail Making, CANTAB, Rey AVLT) analysed as age-38 scores adjusted for childhood IQ; informant-rated attention and memory problems at 38. Ordinary least-squares linear-trend regressions across five exposure groups, adjusted for sex, with sensitivity analyses excluding recent cannabis use, persistent tobacco, hard-drug or alcohol dependence and schizophrenia, an education-adjusted model, and analyses by age of onset and by frequency of use in the year before testing. Analytic sample 874.
can_establish: Whether, in a population birth cohort first tested before cannabis use began, people with more waves of cannabis dependence between 18 and 38 lost more IQ relative to their own childhood scores than people who never used cannabis, and whether this held after excluding recent use, other persistent substance dependence and schizophrenia, and after adjusting for education.
cannot_establish: That cannabis caused the decline, because change scores remove stable childhood differences but not influences that act over time (childhood SES, family environment, self-control and conduct problems are not adjusted in this paper), exposure is self-reported without biological checks, the adolescent-onset and cessation findings rest on 12 to 23 people per cell without a test of interaction, and the group described as having stopped had used cannabis on up to 52 days in the past year.

sample.recruitment: Population birth cohort: all consecutive births in Dunedin, New Zealand, between 1 April 1972 and 31 March 1973; 1,037 children (91% of eligible births; 52% boys) constituted at age 3, covering the range of socioeconomic status of the South Island and primarily of white European ancestry; assessed at 3, 5, 7, 9, 11, 13, 15, 18, 21, 26, 32 and 38 (Methods › Participants, 1st paragraph).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Members with missing data at 3 or more of the 5 cannabis waves were excluded from the exposure variables; 97% of living members were classified (83% with no missing wave, 11% with one, 3% with two) (Methods › Measures › Cannabis use, 1st paragraph). For the 7 members who had tried cannabis by 13, childhood IQ was averaged over ages 7, 9 and 11 only (Methods › Statistical Analysis, 1st paragraph). The analytic sample is 874 (the Table 1 groups sum to 874, and the Fig. 1 key, read by the first reader only, gives the full birth cohort as n=874); how the other assessed members dropped out of the IQ analysis is not stated in the main text.
sample.demographics: Percentage male is higher in the dependence groups: 38.84% (never used), 49.48% (used, never dependent), 70.00% (1 wave), 62.86% (2 waves), 81.58% (3 or more waves). Mean childhood full-scale IQ 99.84, 102.32, 96.40, 102.14 and 99.68 in the same groups (Table 1). No other characteristic (childhood or family SES, ethnicity, conduct problems, personality) is tabulated by exposure group.
sample.attrition: At 38, 96% of the 1,004 living members were assessed (2010–2012); the 4% not seen at 38 were not more likely to have been cannabis dependent at 18 (F = 2.22, P = 0.14), and attrition is described as non-cumulative (Methods › Participants, 1st and 2nd paragraphs). Informant reports were analysed for 822 (Table 5). Editors' arithmetic: 96% of 1,004 is about 964, so about 90 members assessed at 38 are not in the analytic sample of 874, for reasons not given in the main text.
sample.selection_effects: Little risk of selection into the cohort (population birth cohort, 96% retention at 38). The exposure groups are formed by behaviour: the never-used group is 28% of the analytic sample (242 of 874, editors' arithmetic), mostly women, and its IQ rose slightly; the most persistent group (38 people) is 82% men. Movement into persistent dependence probably tracks childhood and family characteristics that this paper does not report by group.

exposure.measurement: Prospective interviews at ages 18, 21, 26, 32 and 38: past-year cannabis dependence by DSM criteria (DSM-III-R and DSM-IV are cited) on the Diagnostic Interview Schedule, and the self-reported number of days of cannabis use in the past year (0–365). No biological verification; the authors argue under-reporting is unlikely given the cohort's long confidentiality record and that misclassification would weaken differences (Discussion, 4th paragraph). Cannabis use in the past 24 hours and past week was self-reported on the testing day at 38 (Methods › Measures › Control variables).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Persistence = number of waves out of 5 with dependence (main exposure) or with use on 4 or more days a week (regular use; weighted κ between the two groupings = 0.77). Adolescent onset = dependence diagnosed before 18 (Fig. 2) or at least weekly use before 18 (Fig. S1 and Fig. 3); the two definitions agree with κ = 0.64. Frequency at 38 (Fig. 3, people with 2 or more waves of dependence only): infrequent = weekly or less in the past year (median 14 days, range 0–52, adolescent onset; median 6 days, range 0–52, adult onset); frequent = median 365 days (range 100–365). Amount per occasion, route and potency were not measured; the authors cite police-seizure data that cannabis potency in New Zealand was similar to that in the United States (Discussion, 4th paragraph).
exposure.polysubstance: Persistent tobacco, hard-drug (heroin, cocaine, amphetamines, for example) and alcohol dependence were diagnosed at the same waves. Handled by exclusion, one at a time (persistent = dependence at 3 or more waves; excluded n=126 tobacco, 7 hard drugs, 53 alcohol; Fig. 1 key, read by the first reader only), and in one multivariable regression with past-24-hour cannabis use, the number of waves with tobacco, hard-drug or alcohol dependence, and schizophrenia (t = −2.20, P = 0.0282, against t = −4.45 adjusted for sex only); the adjusted coefficient is not reported. Use of alcohol and other drugs short of dependence was not modelled.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not required. Use in the past 24 hours (n=38) and past week (n=89) at testing was self-reported and excluded in sensitivity analyses (sizes from the Fig. 1 key, read by the first reader only). In the cessation analysis the "infrequent" group had used cannabis on 0 to 52 days in the year before testing (Fig. 3 legend), so it is not a group abstinent for a year.

comparison.controls: Cohort members who never used cannabis at any of the five waves (n=242), and members who used but never met dependence criteria (n=479); each person's childhood IQ is also their own baseline.
comparison.matching: None. Sex is a covariate in every model; childhood IQ differences are handled by analysing change (full-scale IQ and subtests) or by adjusting age-38 scores for childhood IQ (residualized change) (Methods › Statistical Analysis).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Childhood IQ is measured before use (only 7 members had tried cannabis by 13). Not adjusted in this paper: childhood or family SES, parental characteristics, childhood self-control or personality, conduct problems, attention problems, family psychiatric history and genetic liability; the authors state that an unknown third variable could account for the findings (Discussion, 3rd paragraph). Tests other than IQ have no childhood baseline.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Not described for the never-used group; other substance dependence enters only through the exclusion analyses and the one multivariable model.

outcomes.instruments: Childhood: WISC-R full-scale IQ averaged over ages 7, 9, 11 and 13. Age 38: WAIS-IV (full-scale, verbal and performance IQ, subtests, and the four index scores), WMS-III (Months of the Year Backward; Verbal Paired Associates), Trail-Making Test B, CANTAB (Rapid Visual Information Processing, Visual Paired Associates Learning, 5-choice reaction time) and the Rey Auditory Verbal Learning Test; informant checklists mailed to people the study member nominated: attention problems (4 items, internal consistency 0.79) and memory problems (3 items, 0.64). Testing in the morning in two counterbalanced 50-minute sessions (Methods › Measures › Neuropsychological functioning, 1st and 2nd paragraphs).
outcomes.validity_norms: WISC-R and WAIS-IV are both scaled to mean 100 and SD 15 (different test versions with different norms); the other tests were normed within the cohort (Methods › Neuropsychological functioning, 1st paragraph). Change scores are IQ points divided by 15 (editors' check: dividing the Table 1 changes by 15 reproduces the printed SD units), and Cohen's benchmarks of 0.2, 0.5 and 0.8 are applied to them.
outcomes.operationalization: Decline = within-person change from childhood to 38 on IQ tests given at both ages. For tests given only at 38, impairment = lower age-38 score adjusted for childhood full-scale IQ, so decline on memory, executive and speed tests is inferred, not measured. Everyday problems = informant ratings adjusted for childhood IQ.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. 28 outcome rows are tested in Tables 2, 3 and 5 (10 IQ scores and subtests, 16 age-38 tests, 2 informant scales), each at P < 0.05, under two exposure definitions (the regular-use results are in Table S1, not read) and in subgroup analyses. Editors' calculation: at a Bonferroni threshold of 0.05/28 (about 0.0018), 8 of the 28 remain significant (full-scale IQ, verbal IQ, Vocabulary, Digit Symbol Coding, Months of the Year Backward, Processing Speed Index, and informant-rated attention and memory problems).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not reported for testers. Informants were chosen by the study members and were not blinded; whether they knew of the study member's cannabis use is not reported.

analysis.effect_sizes: Full-scale IQ change in SD units by waves of dependence: never used +0.05; used, never dependent −0.07; 1 wave −0.11; 2 waves −0.17; 3 or more waves −0.38 (mean 99.68 to 93.93, a loss of 5.75 points, editors' arithmetic); linear trend t = −4.45, P < 0.0001, adjusted for sex (Tables 1 and 2). Regular use: +0.05, −0.07, −0.20, −0.13 and −0.35 (96.00 to 90.77 in the 41 people with regular use at 3 or more waves) (Table 1). Trend without the 3-or-more group: t = −2.94, P = 0.0034. Adjusted for education: t = −3.41, P = 0.0007; among people with high-school education or less, the 3-or-more group changed by −0.48 (n=26) against −0.03 for those who never used (n=59), trend t = −3.36, P = 0.0009 (Table 4). Multivariable adjustment for past-24-hour use, other dependence and schizophrenia: t = −2.20, P = 0.0282. No regression coefficients or confidence intervals are reported, only group means in SD units and t statistics. Age-38 tests adjusted for childhood IQ, 3-or-more group: Months of the Year Backward −0.63 (t = −5.24), Processing Speed Index −0.61 (t = −3.64), Rey total recall −0.48 (t = −2.65), Rapid Visual Information Processing A prime −0.45 (t = −2.58); 7 of 16 tests not significant (Table 3). Informant ratings, 3-or-more group: attention problems +0.96 SD and memory problems +0.75 SD (t = 7.74 and 7.65) (Table 5). Adolescent-onset against adult-onset dependence (rendered Fig. 2; group sizes and p values printed on the figure, bar heights read approximately): 1 wave about −0.22 (n=17) vs −0.08 (n=57), p = .44; 2 waves about −0.39 (n=12) vs −0.03 (n=21), p = .09; 3 or more waves about −0.54 (n=23; the legend gives about −0.55, or 8 points) vs −0.14 (n=14), p = .02.
analysis.covariates: Sex in all models. Childhood IQ through change scores, or as a covariate for the age-38-only tests. Education in one model; past-24-hour cannabis use, number of waves with tobacco, hard-drug and alcohol dependence, and schizophrenia in one multivariable model. No socioeconomic, family or personality covariates in this paper.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No registration or analysis plan reported; six hypotheses are stated in the introduction (Introduction, 5th paragraph).
analysis.selective_reporting: Every test in Tables 2, 3 and 5 is reported, including non-significant ones. Not reported: adjusted coefficients and confidence intervals (only t and P); in the main text, the regular-use parallel analyses, the exclusion analyses by subtest and the weekly-use definition of adolescent onset, which are in supplements (Tables S1, S2, Fig. S1; not read). The adolescent-onset contrast is shown as stratum-specific p values in a figure without a test of interaction, and the cessation comparisons are child-versus-adult tests within each group only.
analysis.power: Not addressed. The most exposed groups are small: 38 people dependent at 3 or more waves; 12 to 23 per adolescent-onset cell in Fig. 2; 13 to 20 per cell in the cessation analysis (Fig. 3).

interpretation_gap.results_show: In this birth cohort, full-scale IQ fell with the number of waves of cannabis dependence: by 0.38 SD (about 6 points) in the 38 people dependent at 3 or more waves, against a rise of 0.05 SD in the 242 who never used, with a linear trend that held after excluding recent use, other persistent dependence or schizophrenia one at a time and after adjusting for education, though the trend statistic halved when recent use, other dependence and schizophrenia were adjusted together (t from −4.45 to −2.20). Declines appeared on 7 of 10 IQ scores, and age-38 scores adjusted for childhood IQ were lower on 9 of 16 other tests. The adolescent-onset contrast was significant only in the 3-or-more stratum (23 against 14 people, p = .02). In the cessation analysis, the 17 people with persistent dependence and adolescent onset who used weekly or less in the past year had a lower adult than childhood IQ (p = .03, Fig. 3).
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract reports decline broadly across domains, impairment concentrated among people whose use began in adolescence, and no full restoration after cessation, and calls the findings "suggestive of a neurotoxic effect of cannabis on the adolescent brain" (Abstract). Gaps: (1) decline was measured only for IQ; the memory, executive and speed tests have no childhood baseline, and 3 of the 7 IQ subtests (Arithmetic, Block Design, Picture Completion) showed no decline in the most persistent group, so the word global rests largely on a non-significant test of equal association across the four WAIS-IV indexes (Δχ2 = 2.13, df = 3, P = 0.55) in small groups; (2) the discussion says impairment was still evident after cessation of use for a year or more (Discussion, 2nd paragraph), but the group in Fig. 3 had used cannabis on up to 52 days in the past year, the limitations paragraph calls them people who quit or reduced their use, and their change is not compared with that of the never-used group; the cessation analysis covers full-scale IQ only, not neuropsychological functioning in general; (3) the statement on adolescent onset rests on one significant stratum of 23 people with no interaction test; (4) the claim that the prospective design ruled out premorbid deficit (Discussion, 2nd paragraph) holds for stable IQ differences only, not for confounders that act over time, as the limitations paragraph concedes; (5) the 8-point figure in the policy paragraph and the Author Summary refers to the 23 adolescent-onset people with 3 or more waves, read from a figure, while the tabulated loss for the 3-or-more group is 5.75 points. Against this, the limitations paragraph states plainly that the data cannot show the association is causal.

timeline.event: Fried, Watkinson & Gray (Neurotoxicology and Teratology): the only earlier prospective study of cannabis and neuropsychological change that Meier et al. identify, described by them as small and with about 2 years of regular use on average (Introduction, 4th paragraph).

This study (PNAS, online 27 August, issue of 2 October 2012), published with a commentary in the same issue titled Long-term effects of adolescent-onset and persistent use of cannabis (p. 15970; not read).

Rogeberg (PNAS 110:4251–4254): a simulation in which SES drives both cannabis exposure and IQ change, with no effect of cannabis, produces results like the main table; argues the estimates are likely biased and proposes further analyses of the cohort (card sc_rogeberg_2013).

Daly, letter proposing that personality (conscientiousness) may explain the association (PNAS 110:E979; listed in the article notes; not read). The authors' reply describes it as a test in the National Child Development Study with personality measured at age 50.

Moffitt, Meier, Caspi & Poulton, reply (PNAS 110:E980–E982): SES did not predict adolescent-onset dependence or IQ change, and the trend estimate was unchanged after adjusting for SES or for childhood self-control and among the 553 people from middle-class families (card sc_moffitt_2013).
A rejoinder titled Reply to Moffitt et al.: Causal inference from observational data remains difficult (PNAS 110:E983), listed in the article notes; not read.

Jackson et al. (PNAS 113:E500–E508), two US twin cohorts (n=789 and 2,277): ever use of cannabis by 17–20 went with a 3.4–4.0-point greater fall in age-standardized Vocabulary, but within twin pairs discordant for use no difference was significant; the authors attribute the association to familial confounding (card sc_jackson_2016).

Meier et al. (Addiction), a longitudinal co-twin control study of adolescent cannabis use and neuropsychological decline, in the project's Tier A list and carded in this round by another reader; not read for this card.

replication.where_it_stands: The association in Dunedin between persistent cannabis dependence and IQ decline is not disputed as a finding; its cause is. The original authors' further analyses found it unchanged after adjustment for childhood SES or self-control, each added alone (Moffitt et al., 2013), while two US twin cohorts with lighter and shorter exposure found an ever-use association with vocabulary decline that was not significant within discordant twin pairs (Jackson et al., 2016), with monozygotic-pair intervals that still include the between-family difference. Later cohort and co-twin studies in the project's lists (Mokrysz et al., 2016; Meier et al., 2018; Schaefer et al., 2022; Meier et al., 2022) are needed before a claim says where the question stands; none is read here.

funding.funder: The Dunedin Multidisciplinary Health and Development Research Unit is supported by the New Zealand Health Research Council; the research was supported by UK Medical Research Council Grants G0100527 and MR/K00381X/1, US National Institute on Aging Grant AG032282, US National Institute of Mental Health Grant MH077874 and US National Institute on Drug Abuse Grant P30 DA023026, with additional support from the Jacobs Foundation (Acknowledgments).
funding.declared_conflicts: "The authors declare no conflict of interest." (Footnotes). PNAS Direct Submission, edited by Michael I. Posner (University of Oregon); received 23 April 2012, approved 30 July 2012 (author information).
funding.affiliations_note: Authors at Duke University, the Institute of Psychiatry at King's College London and the Dunedin unit of the University of Otago. M.H.M., A.C. and T.E.M. designed the research and wrote the paper; T.E.M., M.H.M. and A.C. also wrote the reply to its critics (Moffitt et al., 2013). A flag for closer reading, not a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: A large prospective cohort, or a co-twin or sibling study within one, that measures IQ and the other tests before, during and after adolescent cannabis use, adjusts jointly for family SES, self-control, conduct problems, family psychiatric history and other substance use, verifies exposure biologically and records potency, and retests people after sustained, verified abstinence, with enough people with persistent adolescent-onset dependence to estimate the interaction with age of onset.

domains.note: Main models adjust for sex only; change scores remove stable childhood IQ differences but not factors that affect IQ over time and predict persistent dependence (family SES, family environment, self-control, conduct problems, genetic liability), none of which is adjusted in this paper. Other dependence is handled by one-at-a-time exclusion and one multivariable model in which the trend statistic halves, without a reported coefficient; education may be a mediator, as the authors note.

Prospective structured diagnoses at five waves, a strength; but self-reported, not verified, with past-year windows that leave gaps between waves, no measure of amount or potency, and two definitions of adolescent onset that agree only moderately (κ = 0.64).
Population birth cohort with 91% of eligible births and 96% retention at 38; exposure groups are defined by behaviour after baseline, which is a confounding rather than a selection problem.
No relevant interventions; changes in use after exposure are part of the exposure definition.

874 of about 964 members assessed at 38 are analysed, without a flow of the exclusions in the main text; people with 3 or more missing cannabis waves excluded; attrition at 38 not related to dependence at 18 (F = 2.22, P = 0.14).

Standardized tests, but childhood and adult IQ come from different Wechsler versions; testers' blinding to cannabis history not reported; informants were nominated by study members and not blinded, and the memory scale's internal consistency is 0.64.

All outcome rows are shown, but 28 outcomes and two exposure definitions are tested without correction, the subgroup findings that carry the abstract rest on small cells and figure-level p values, and adjusted coefficients are not reported.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: ROBINS-E overall is no milder than the worst domain. The design is strong in what it controls: a population birth cohort, prospective exposure and IQ measured before use, so stable childhood IQ differences cannot explain the change scores. What this paper does not control is any factor that changes IQ over time and also predicts persistent dependence; the one multivariable model roughly halved the trend statistic and its coefficient is not given, and the headline subgroup findings rest on very small cells. Citable for IQ change by exposure group as tabulated, for robustness to the stated exclusions and to education, and for the authors' own limits; not for a causal or neurotoxic effect, for decline on tests without a childhood baseline, for persistence after a year without use, or for the size of an adjusted association.

key_findings.finding: Dunedin birth cohort of 1,037 (91% of eligible births), 96% of 1,004 living members assessed at 38; cannabis dependence and frequency assessed at 18, 21, 26, 32 and 38; IQ tested at 7, 9, 11 and 13, when only 7 members had tried cannabis, and again at 38.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Participants, 1st paragraph; Methods › Measures › Cannabis use, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Methods › Measures › Neuropsychological functioning, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Full-scale IQ, childhood to 38, by waves of cannabis dependence: never used 99.84 to 100.64 (+0.05 SD, n=242); used, never dependent 102.32 to 101.25 (−0.07, n=479); 1 wave 96.40 to 94.78 (−0.11, n=80); 2 waves 102.14 to 99.67 (−0.17, n=35); 3 or more waves 99.68 to 93.93 (−0.38, n=38). By waves of regular use (4 or more days a week): 3 or more waves 96.00 to 90.77 (−0.35, n=41). The paper converts −0.38 SD to about 6 IQ points.
key_findings.locator: Results › Do Study Members with More Persistent Cannabis Use Show Greater IQ Decline?, 1st paragraph; Table 1
key_findings.note: SD units are the raw IQ change divided by 15 (editors' check: 5.75/15 = 0.383), so the group values are unadjusted; only the trend tests are adjusted for sex. Men are 81.58% of the 3-or-more dependence group against 38.84% of the never-used group; sex is a covariate in the trend tests.

key_findings.finding: Linear trend of full-scale IQ change with waves of dependence, adjusted for sex: t = −4.45, P < 0.0001; verbal IQ t = −4.15; performance IQ t = −2.84, P = 0.0046. Subtests declining significantly: Information, Similarities, Vocabulary, Digit Symbol Coding (3-or-more group −0.62, t = −5.60); not declining: Arithmetic (3-or-more group +0.06, P = 0.47), Block Design (+0.02, P = 0.58), Picture Completion (+0.15, P = 0.24).
key_findings.locator: Results › Do Study Members with More Persistent Cannabis Use Show Greater IQ Decline?, 2nd paragraph; Table 2

key_findings.finding: The trend remained when the 38 people with 3 or more waves of dependence were excluded (t = −2.94, P = 0.0034).
key_findings.locator: Results › Do Study Members with More Persistent Cannabis Use Show Greater IQ Decline?, 3rd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Tests given only at 38, adjusted for childhood IQ and sex: 9 of 16 showed a significant trend with persistence of dependence (for the 3-or-more group, for example, Months of the Year Backward −0.63, t = −5.24; Processing Speed Index −0.61, t = −3.64; Rey total recall −0.48, t = −2.65; Working Memory Index −0.16, t = −2.16, P = 0.0311), while Trail-Making B (P = 0.25), Verbal Paired Associates (P = 0.14 and 0.29), choice reaction time (P = 0.71) and three other measures did not. Associations with the four WAIS-IV indexes could be equated without loss of fit (Δχ2 = 2.13, df = 3, P = 0.55), which the authors read as impairment not differing between domains.
key_findings.locator: Results › Is Impairment Specific to Certain Neuropsychological Domains or Is It Global?, 1st paragraph; Table 3
key_findings.note: These tests have no childhood baseline; the effects are age-38 differences adjusted for childhood IQ, not measured declines. Two of the nine significant scores are the WAIS-IV Perceptual Reasoning (t = −2.33) and Verbal Comprehension (t = −3.04) indexes, so the executive, memory and speed scores alone give 7 of 14; no correction for testing 16 scores (see outcomes.multiplicity_correction).

key_findings.finding: Excluding in turn people who used cannabis in the 24 hours (n=38) or week (n=89) before testing, or with persistent tobacco (n=126), hard-drug (n=7) or alcohol (n=53) dependence, or with schizophrenia (n=28), left the IQ change estimates virtually the same and significant. In one multivariable regression adjusting for past-24-hour use, number of waves with tobacco, hard-drug or alcohol dependence, and schizophrenia, the trend remained significant at t = −2.20, P = 0.0282.
key_findings.locator: Results › Is Impairment Attributable to Persistent Cannabis Use or Are There Alternative Explanations?, 1st paragraph; Fig. 1 and its legend
key_findings.note: The excluded group sizes (38, 89, 126, 7, 53, 28) and the full-cohort n of 874 are printed only in the Fig. 1 key, an image read by the first reader; the second reader and the adjudicator could not view it (figure image not viewable), so these sizes are single-reader values, although 874 matches the Table 1 total. Bar values were not extracted. The multivariable t is about half the sex-adjusted t (−4.45), and no coefficient is given, so the size of the adjusted association cannot be recovered.

key_findings.finding: The trend remained significant after adjusting for years of education (t = −3.41, P = 0.0007, against −4.45 before); fewer people with persistent dependence studied beyond high school (χ2 = 63.94, P < 0.0001); among people with high-school education or less, IQ change was −0.03 (never used, n=59), −0.14 (n=130), −0.16 (n=43), −0.25 (n=20) and −0.48 (3 or more waves, n=26), trend t = −3.36, P = 0.0009.
key_findings.locator: Results › Is Impairment Apparent Even After Controlling for Years of Education?, 1st paragraph; Table 4
key_findings.note: The authors say adjusting for education is likely an overcontrol if cannabis lowers schooling (Discussion, 3rd paragraph).

key_findings.finding: Informants nominated by study members rated more attention and memory problems with persistence of dependence, adjusted for childhood IQ: attention −0.21 (never used, n=228) to +0.96 SD (3 or more waves, n=35), t = 7.74; memory −0.27 to +0.75 SD, t = 7.65; both P < 0.0001. Scales: 4 attention items (internal consistency 0.79) and 3 memory items (0.64).
key_findings.locator: Results › Does Cannabis-Associated Neuropsychological Impairment Translate into Functional Problems in Daily Life?, 1st paragraph; Table 5; Methods › Measures › Neuropsychological functioning, 2nd paragraph
key_findings.note: Informants were not blinded, and whether they knew of the study member's cannabis use is not reported.

key_findings.finding: Holding the number of dependence waves equal, people whose dependence began before 18 declined more than people whose dependence began in adulthood; the difference was significant only at 3 or more waves: 1 wave about −0.22 SD (n=17) vs −0.08 (n=57), p = .44; 2 waves about −0.39 (n=12) vs −0.03 (n=21), p = .09; 3 or more waves about −0.54 (n=23) vs −0.14 (n=14), p = .02. The legend converts about −0.55 SD in the adolescent-onset 3-or-more group to 8 IQ points. The authors state that people whose dependence began in adulthood did not appear to decline with persistence; with onset defined as weekly use before 18 the results were similar (Fig. S1, not read).
key_findings.locator: Results › Are Adolescent Cannabis Users Particularly Vulnerable?, 1st paragraph; Fig. 2 and its legend
key_findings.note: Group sizes and p values are printed on the rendered Fig. 2; bar heights were read approximately. The p values are printed between the onset groups at each persistence level (p = .02 is the printed between-onset test at 3 or more waves); the Methods describe only the trend tests, so which test gives them, and whether it is adjusted for sex, is not stated. No test of the interaction between age of onset and persistence is reported. The Fig. 2 groups total 144, against 153 people with 1 or more waves of dependence in Table 1.

key_findings.finding: Among people with persistent dependence (2 or more waves), split by onset of weekly use before 18 and by frequency of use in the year before testing at 38: adolescent onset, infrequent use (weekly or less; median 14 days, range 0–52; n=17) childhood to adult IQ p = .03 (about 102 to 97.5); adolescent onset, frequent use (median 365 days; n=19) p = .0002 (about 97 to 89); adult onset, infrequent (median 6 days; n=13) p = .73 (about 104 to 105); adult onset, frequent (n=20) p = .11 (about 98.5 to 95.5). The authors conclude that cessation did not fully restore functioning in people whose use began in adolescence.
key_findings.locator: Results › What Is the Effect of Cessation of Cannabis Use?, 1st paragraph; Fig. 3 and its legend
key_findings.note: Group sizes and p values are printed on the rendered Fig. 3; IQ values were read approximately from the bars. The p values compare each group's own childhood and adult IQ by a test the Methods do not describe; onset here means at least weekly use before 18 (panel labels), not dependence before 18; no comparison with the never-used group's change (+0.8 points) or between the infrequent and frequent groups is reported. The "infrequent" group includes people who used on up to 52 days in the past year.

key_findings.finding: The authors state that their data cannot show whether the association is causal and that an unknown third variable could account for it; they propose a neurotoxic effect of adolescent cannabis use as one hypothesis and note that adjusting for education is likely an overcontrol if cannabis leads to school dropout.

Cannabis dependence and frequency were self-reported without biological validation; the authors argue under-reporting is unlikely and that misclassification would weaken group differences; they call for research on whether impairment is reversible, and note that the findings are limited to one cohort born in Dunedin in the 1970s.

The Author Summary describes the people with the most persistent use as n=41 losing an average of 5–6 IQ points (the regular-use grouping, Table P1) and people with adolescent onset who used persistently to 38 as n=23 losing an average of 8 IQ points.
key_findings.locator: Author Summary (printed p. 15980), questions i and iv; Table P1
key_findings.note: Three figures for the most persistent group circulate: 5.75 points (3 or more waves of dependence, n=38, Table 1), 5.2 points (3 or more waves of regular use, n=41, Table 1 and Table P1) and 8 points (adolescent-onset dependence at 3 or more waves, n=23, read from Fig. 2).

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract states that neuropsychological testing was done at 13, before cannabis use, and again at 38; in the Methods only IQ was tested in childhood (averaged over 7, 9, 11 and 13), and the memory, executive and speed tests were given only at 38.
reporting_issues.consequence: Decline can be claimed for IQ only; for the other tests the paper shows age-38 differences adjusted for childhood IQ.

reporting_issues.issue: The discussion says impairment was still evident after cessation of use for a year or more (Discussion, 2nd paragraph), while the group so described used cannabis on 0 to 52 days in the past year (Fig. 3 legend), and the limitations paragraph calls them people who quit or reduced their use (Discussion, 4th paragraph).
reporting_issues.consequence: The data show decline in people who used weekly or less in the year before testing, not after a year of abstinence; a claim on persistence after stopping cannot rest on this analysis.

reporting_issues.issue: Adolescent onset is defined as dependence before 18 in the vulnerability analysis (Fig. 2) but as weekly use before 18 in the cessation analysis (Fig. 3); the two definitions agree with κ = 0.64 (Results › Are Adolescent Cannabis Users Particularly Vulnerable?, 1st paragraph).
reporting_issues.consequence: The two adolescent-onset findings concern overlapping but different groups and should not be combined in one statement.

reporting_issues.issue: Group sizes in the figures do not add up to the table: the Fig. 2 groups total 144 against 153 people with 1, 2 or 3 or more waves of dependence in Table 1, and the Fig. 3 groups total 69 against 73 people with 2 or more waves; the analytic sample of 874 is not reconciled with the about 964 members assessed at 38 (editors' arithmetic).
reporting_issues.consequence: Small unexplained losses in the subgroup analyses, which matter when cells hold 12 to 23 people.

reporting_issues.issue: Only t statistics and P values are reported for the adjusted models; the multivariable model's t (−2.20) is about half the sex-adjusted t (−4.45), and the abstract mentions only the education adjustment.
reporting_issues.consequence: The size of the association after adjustment for other dependence, recent use and schizophrenia is unknown; claims should quote the group means and say that adjusted estimates are reported only as test statistics.

reporting_issues.issue: The Table 3 legend says persistent dependence was associated with impairment in each of five areas, and the abstract calls the decline broad across domains; but the one perceptual-reasoning measure at 38 is the WAIS-IV index (t = −2.33), the perceptual subtests with a childhood baseline (Block Design, Picture Completion) did not decline (Table 2), and 7 of 16 age-38 tests were not significant (Table 3).
reporting_issues.consequence: The evidence supports decline on several verbal and speed measures and on full-scale IQ, not a uniform decline across all functions.

reporting_issues.issue: The Author Summary quotes n=41 losing 5–6 points (regular-use grouping) while the main text uses the dependence grouping (n=38, 5.75 points), and the 8-point figure repeated in the policy paragraph comes from 23 people read off a figure.
reporting_issues.consequence: Secondary sources relay different figures for the same idea; claims must name the grouping, the n and the source of each figure.
